title: Problem Solving
blurb: Breaking hard problems into tractable pieces — compounds with everything.

beginner: Work a small example by hand

lessons.title: The method
lessons.explain: Strong problem-solvers don't code first. They: (1) restate the problem, (2) work a tiny example by hand, (3) find the pattern/tool, (4) write brute force, (5) optimize, (6) explain the trade-offs.

lessons.title: Understanding the problem first
objectives: Restate a problem and ask clarifying questions before solving it
Explain how restat changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect restat with clarifying questions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Restating a problem in your own words surfaces misunderstandings early, before any code is written to fix the wrong problem. Ambiguous problems often have several valid interpretations -- asking clarifying questions before diving in avoids solving the wrong one.
examples:
# before writing any code:
# 1. restate the problem in your own words
# 2. ask: what's the input range? what should happen on empty input?
# 3. define done: 'this function returns X for input Y, handling Z edge case'
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to code before confirming you understand what's actually being asked -- this can waste significant effort solving the wrong problem.
lessons.careerRelevance: Interviewers and real projects both reward this step -- it's often what's actually being evaluated.

# 1. restate the problem in your own words

lessons.title: Working examples & brute force first
objectives: Use small examples and a brute-force solution before optimizing
Explain how small example changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect small example with brute force and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Working through a small example by hand helps you discover the actual pattern needed, and gives you a test case to check against.
examples:
# example: 'find the longest streak of a repeated number'
# work a tiny example by hand first: [3,3,3,5,5] -> streak of 3, length 3
# THEN write the brute-force version: check every position, count how far the streak goes
commonMistakes: Trying to write the optimal, clever solution immediately -- without a working brute-force baseline, it's hard to tell if the 'clever' version is even correct.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is one of the most reliable, transferable problem-solving habits across any domain.
lessons.explain: Working through a small example by hand helps you discover the actual pattern needed, and gives you a test case to check against.

lessons.title: Breaking problems down
objectives: Split a problem into smaller subproblems, and reduce it to a known pattern
Explain how subproblems changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect subproblems with divide and conquer and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Breaking a problem into smaller subproblems makes each piece easier to reason about, implement, and test independently. Divide and conquer is a specific version of this: split into smaller, similar subproblems, solve each, then combine the results.
examples:
# instead of solving 'sort and deduplicate and count' all at once:
# subproblem 1: sort the list
# subproblem 2: remove duplicates from the sorted list
# subproblem 3: count what's left
# each piece is small enough to get right and test on its own
commonMistakes: Trying to solve a large, multi-part problem in one single pass instead of splitting it into independently checkable pieces.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the core strategy behind managing any large, complex real project, not just small exercises.
lessons.explain: Breaking a problem into smaller subproblems makes each piece easier to reason about, implement, and test independently. Divide and conquer is a specific version of this: split into smaller, similar subproblems, solve each, then combine the results.

# subproblem 1: sort the list
# subproblem 2: remove duplicates from the sorted list
# subproblem 3: count what's left
# each piece is small enough to get right and test on its own

lessons.title: Constraints & complexity
objectives: Identify constraints and reason about time complexity
Explain how constraints changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect constraints with time complexity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Identifying constraints (input size, time limit, edge cases) before choosing an approach matters because they determine which approaches are even feasible -- an O(n^2) approach might be fine for small inputs but impractical for millions of records.
examples:
# a solution that's O(n^2) might run instantly on 100 items
# but take minutes or crash on 10 million items --
# always ask: what's the REAL expected input size?
commonMistakes: Ignoring stated or implied constraints (input size, time limits) when choosing an approach, only to discover the solution doesn't scale.
lessons.careerRelevance: Complexity reasoning is one of the most consistently tested skills in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Edge cases & verification
objectives: Test against edge cases and verify your solution by hand
Explain how edge cases changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect edge cases with verify and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An edge case is an input at the boundary of what's expected -- empty, zero, negative, maximum size, duplicates -- easy to overlook but a common source of real bugs. Testing your solution against these edge cases, not just the 'normal' example, catches algorithms that work for typical input but silently fail at boundaries.
examples:
# always explicitly test:
# - empty input: []
# - a single element: [5]
# - duplicates: [3,3,3]
# - the largest size you're told to expect
commonMistakes: Testing only the 'normal' example from the problem statement and skipping empty/boundary cases entirely.
lessons.careerRelevance: Edge-case awareness is one of the most commonly checked-for habits in code review and interviews alike.

lessons.title: Communication & problem-solving habits
objectives: Think aloud, use diagrams, and track what you've tried
Explain how thinking aloud changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect thinking aloud with explaining your reasoning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Explaining your reasoning out loud (in an interview or otherwise) makes your thought process visible, which is often what's actually being evaluated, and can surface your own reasoning gaps. Drawing a diagram or table can reveal a problem's structure faster than abstract reasoning alone.
examples:
# habits that compound:
# - narrate your thinking, even the uncertain parts
# - sketch the data structure or flow on paper before coding
# - jot down 'tried X, didn't work because Y' so you don't repeat it
commonMistakes: Going completely silent while thinking, especially under observation (like an interview) -- this leaves the listener with no way to help or evaluate your approach.
lessons.careerRelevance: These communication habits are frequently what actually differentiates similarly-skilled candidates.

lessons.title: After solving: reflection & careful translation
objectives: Reflect after solving, and translate your idea into code carefully
Explain how translating changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect translating with reflection and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A common mistake is rushing the translation of a working idea into code, introducing small implementation bugs (off-by-one, wrong variable) that don't reflect any flaw in the actual idea. After solving, briefly reflecting on what made it hard, and whether a simpler or more general approach existed, compounds your skill over time.
examples:
# after solving:
# - did I translate the idea into code carefully, or rush it?
# - what made this hard? would I recognize this pattern faster next time?
# - could I explain this solution clearly to someone else right now?
commonMistakes: Treating a problem as 'done' the instant it passes, without any reflection on whether the approach was accidental or genuinely understood.
lessons.careerRelevance: This reflection habit is what turns solving many problems into actually getting better over time, rather than just repeating effort.

lessons.title: Heuristics & simplifying first
objectives: Use heuristics and simplified versions to make progress on hard problems
Explain how heuristic changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect heuristic with simplest and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A heuristic is a practical rule-of-thumb approach that often works well, even without a guarantee of the best possible result. Starting with the SIMPLEST possible version of a problem, even if the real problem is more complex, often reveals the core structure needed, which you then extend for the full complexity.
examples:
# simplify first: if the real problem is 'find the best route through 50 cities,'
# first solve it for 3 cities by hand -- the core idea often becomes clear at small scale
commonMistakes: Attempting the full, complex version of a problem directly instead of starting from a deliberately simplified version to find the core idea first.
lessons.careerRelevance: Heuristic thinking and simplification are practical tools used constantly in real-world problem solving, not just academic exercises.

options: start coding
fully understand it & do an example

options: it's slower and adds no value

quiz.q: What is a brute-force solution?
options: a solution that always crashes
a straightforward, often less efficient approach that directly checks all possibilities, prioritizing correctness over speed
an illegal solution in interviews
a solution written in assembly language

quiz.q: Why start with a brute-force solution before optimizing?
options: brute force is always the best final answer
it establishes a correct baseline you can test against and improve incrementally, rather than risking a broken 'clever' solution
it's required by all programming languages
optimized solutions are always wrong

quiz.q: What does breaking a problem into smaller subproblems help with?
options: nothing, it just adds complexity

it's only useful for recursive problems

quiz.q: Why identify constraints (input size, time limit, edge cases) before choosing an approach?
options: constraints never matter
they determine which approaches are even feasible (e.g. an O(n^2) approach may be fine for small inputs but not for millions of records)
constraints are only relevant in coding interviews
identifying constraints is the interviewer's job, not yours

quiz.q: What is an edge case?
options: a case that never actually happens
an input at the boundary of what's expected (empty, zero, negative, maximum size, duplicates) that's easy to overlook
a bug that can't be fixed
a case only relevant to security code

quiz.q: Why explicitly consider edge cases like an empty list or single-element list?
options: they're rare enough to ignore
many real bugs come specifically from these boundary conditions behaving differently than the 'normal' case

quiz.q: What is the benefit of explaining your reasoning out loud while solving a problem (in an interview or otherwise)?
options: no benefit, it's just noise
it makes your thought process visible, which is often what's actually being evaluated, and can surface your own reasoning gaps
it only helps the listener, not you

options: questions make you look unprepared
ambiguous problems often have several valid interpretations, and solving the wrong one wastes all the effort spent
clarifying questions are only for beginners

quiz.q: What does time complexity (e.g. O(n), O(n^2)) describe?
options: the exact number of seconds a program takes
how the amount of work grows relative to the size of the input, at a high level
the number of lines of code
how much memory a variable uses

quiz.q: Why does time complexity matter even if a solution 'works' on small test cases?
options: it doesn't matter if tests pass
an approach that's fine for small inputs can become impractically slow as input size grows, which small tests won't reveal
small test cases always represent the worst case

quiz.q: What is a common strategy when you're stuck and don't know where to start?
options: give up immediately

quiz.q: Why test your solution against the edge cases you identified earlier, not just the 'normal' example?
options: edge cases are guaranteed to work if the normal case does

quiz.q: What is the value of comparing multiple possible approaches before committing to one?
options: there's no value, the first idea is usually best
different approaches trade off differently (speed, memory, complexity, readability), and comparing surfaces the right fit for the actual constraints
comparing approaches wastes valuable time always

quiz.q: Why might a simpler, slightly less efficient solution sometimes be the RIGHT choice over a more complex optimal one?
options: simpler solutions are never acceptable
readability, maintainability, and lower bug risk can outweigh marginal performance gains, especially if the problem's actual scale doesn't need the optimization
efficiency never matters in real projects
simpler code always runs faster too

quiz.q: What does 'divide and conquer' mean as a problem-solving strategy?
options: splitting work between two programmers
breaking a problem into smaller, similar subproblems, solving each, then combining the results
avoiding difficult problems entirely
a specific sorting algorithm only

quiz.q: Why keep track of what you've already tried when working through a hard problem?
options: there's no benefit to tracking attempts
it avoids wasting time re-trying the same failed approach and helps you reason about what's actually different in remaining options
it's only useful for graded assignments

quiz.q: What is the risk of writing code before you fully understand the problem?
options: there's no risk, code can always be adjusted
you may build in the wrong direction, discovering the misunderstanding only after significant wasted effort
code written early is always more efficient

it catches your own misunderstanding of the problem or a logic error early, before investing further
hand computation is always wrong
this step is only needed for math-heavy problems

quiz.q: What does it mean to 'reduce a new problem to one you already know how to solve'?
options: ignoring the new problem entirely
recognizing that the new problem shares structure with a familiar pattern or algorithm, and adapting that known solution

a technique that only works for exam questions

quiz.q: Why is drawing a diagram or table sometimes more useful than jumping straight to code?
options: diagrams are never useful for programming
visualizing the problem's structure (e.g. a graph, a sequence, states) can reveal the right approach faster than abstract reasoning alone
diagrams are only for non-technical people

options: move on immediately, there's nothing more to learn
briefly reflect on what made it hard and whether a simpler or more general approach existed

never revisit solved problems

quiz.q: Why might starting with the SIMPLEST possible version of a problem help, even if the real problem is more complex?
options: it doesn't help, simplifying wastes time
solving a simplified version first often reveals the core structure needed, which you then extend for the full complexity
simplified versions are usually a completely different problem

quiz.q: What is a heuristic, in the context of problem-solving?
options: a guaranteed, provably optimal method
a practical rule-of-thumb approach that often works well, even without a guarantee of the best possible result
a type of programming language

quiz.q: Why explicitly define what 'done' looks like before starting to solve a problem?
options: it's unnecessary, you'll know when you're done

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when translating a working idea into code?
options: there are no common mistakes at this stage
rushing the translation and introducing small implementation bugs (off-by-one, wrong variable) that don't reflect a flaw in the actual idea

What part of the process was skipped, and when should it have happened -- before or after writing the code?

description: Breaking hard problems into tractable pieces — compounds with everything.

interviewPreparation.q: Why do interviewers care about your process, not just whether you get the right answer?
interviewPreparation.a: A correct answer reached by luck or memorization doesn't predict how you'll handle a genuinely novel problem on the job, but a visible, repeatable process (clarify, brute-force first, analyze complexity, check edge cases) does -- it's evidence of a transferable skill, not a one-off result.

interviewPreparation.q: Why write a brute-force solution first, even when you suspect a better approach exists?
interviewPreparation.a: It gives you a working baseline you can verify correctness against, clarifies the problem in concrete terms, and often reveals the actual bottleneck that suggests the optimization -- jumping straight to a clever approach without this baseline risks solving the wrong problem efficiently, or getting stuck with nothing working at all.

interviewPreparation.q: How do stated constraints (like 'n up to 10 million') actually help you choose an approach?
interviewPreparation.a: They let you estimate what complexity is actually required before writing any code -- roughly, 10^8 operations is a reasonable ceiling for typical time limits, so n up to 10 million rules out O(n²) and points toward O(n log n) or better, which narrows down which approaches are even worth attempting.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the risk of only testing your solution on the 'normal' example given in the problem?
interviewPreparation.a: The given example is usually chosen to illustrate the normal case, not to stress-test your solution -- edge cases (empty input, a single element, all duplicates, boundary values) are exactly where solutions that look correct actually fail, and they're often not covered by the example at all.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you handle getting stuck on a problem during an interview?
interviewPreparation.a: Say what you're stuck on out loud rather than going silent, try simplifying to a smaller or more restricted version of the problem first, and revisit your assumptions -- being stuck and communicating about it clearly is a normal, expected part of the process, not a sign you should have already known the answer.

careerApplications: The actual skill coding interviews are trying to measure.

capstone.title: Work a genuinely unfamiliar problem end-to-end, under real interview conditions
capstone.description: Given a problem you haven't seen before (or a Company Path course capstone reframed as an unfamiliar prompt), work through the FULL process deliberately and visibly: restate it in your own words, ask the clarifying questions you'd actually need, write a brute-force solution first, identify the constraints that determine what complexity is actually required, find the edge cases before being surprised by them, and write up your reasoning as if explaining it to an interviewer. This capstone is about the process being visible and repeatable, not just arriving at a correct answer.
deliverables: A written restatement of the problem in your own words, including inputs, outputs, and at least one clarifying question you'd ask
A brute-force solution written first, before any optimization -- with a note on its actual complexity
A stated read of the problem's constraints and what complexity they actually require, justifying whether the brute-force solution is already good enough or needs improving
At least 3 edge cases identified and verified against, found BEFORE being surprised by a failure, not after
A written explanation of your final approach as if talking an interviewer through it, including why you didn't pick a different reasonable-sounding approach
capstone.portfolioTips: This is less a portfolio artifact and more a rehearsal -- the value is in practicing the visible, narrated process itself under real conditions, since that's exactly what a live technical interview is actually evaluating, not just whether the final code is correct.

industryUsage.usage: Technical interviews explicitly evaluate the problem-solving PROCESS -- clarifying questions, brute-force-first reasoning, complexity analysis -- not just whether a candidate eventually reaches a correct answer.
Interview guidance commonly emphasizes reading and using stated constraints to gauge required complexity before writing code, since this is a frequent, visible signal of engineering maturity.
Structured problem-solving communication (restating the problem, thinking aloud, checking edge cases) is explicitly part of what interviewers are trained to evaluate, separate from raw coding speed.
